title: The One With The Hypnosis Tape

jokes.text: What's so funny? Nothing. It's an acting exercise. I'm practicing my fake laugh.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Chandler why he's laughing
jokes.punchline: He claims it's an 'acting exercise' — a transparently absurd cover for something he clearly finds funny
jokes.explanation: A solid opener that uses Chandler's evasive, self-deprecating character voice well. The fake laugh cover is funny but not groundbreaking.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: What's so funny?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: Nothing, I'm just practicing my fake laugh.

jokes.text: Come on, man. At least let me finish this last one. Only if you give me a drag.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to quit smoking and begs to finish his last cigarette
jokes.punchline: Joey, who is supposed to be helping him quit, demands a drag himself — completely undermining the anti-smoking mission
jokes.explanation: A compact, character-true joke. Joey's self-interest instantly deflates the dramatic quit-smoking framing. Works because it's so Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's like a little white horse galloping through my lungs.

jokes.text: Oh, dark mother, once again I suckle at your smoky teat.
jokes.setup: Chandler takes a final drag from a cigarette he's supposedly giving up
jokes.punchline: He delivers a melodramatic, quasi-religious invocation to the cigarette — wildly disproportionate to the mundane act
jokes.explanation: One of the most memorable lines in this episode. The language is hilariously overblown — 'dark mother,' 'suckle,' 'smoky teat' — each word escalating the absurdity. It's original, highly quotable, and could only come from Chandler's particular brand of melodramatic self-awareness. The writing is genuinely exceptional for a sitcom one-liner: it finds maximum comedy in a familiar situation (smoking addiction) through wholly unexpected language. Justifies an 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm quitting smoking. I'm never going to smoke again. This is my last cigarette. I'm throwing away the rest of the pack. I'm done. Forever. No more cigarettes for me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay. Keep the cigarette.

jokes.text: No, why don't you hold on to that one. [Joey returning the cigarette to Chandler after hearing the speech]
jokes.setup: Chandler's bizarre invocation to the cigarette clearly disturbs Joey
jokes.punchline: Joey wordlessly hands the cigarette back — his disgust at Chandler's weirdness is funnier than anything he could say
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the 'dark mother' joke. Joey's reversal — suddenly NOT wanting a drag — is the ideal comedic payoff. Economy is excellent: one short line does all the work. The callback structure earns it a solid score.

jokes.text: Okay, that's like the least fun game ever.
jokes.setup: Monica and the others are watching Chandler's smoking ritual with increasing discomfort
jokes.punchline: Monica sums it up with a flat, dismissive verdict on the 'game' of taking a last drag
jokes.explanation: A functional tag line. It works as a button but it's a generic dismissal line that could fit in dozens of sitcoms. Below-average craft but serviceable.

jokes.text: Nope. That patch is no good.
jokes.setup: Monica introduces what is supposed to be a quitting aid for Chandler
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately and confidently dismisses the nicotine patch with zero explanation — as if she has expert authority she clearly doesn't have
jokes.explanation: A quick Phoebe character beat. The comedy is entirely in her unearned confidence. Works because it's true to Phoebe's voice but isn't developed into anything larger.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I tried quitting by replacing cigarettes with lollipops, but I just ended up looking like a five-year-old at a construction site.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Then I tried acupuncture. The guy stuck needles all over my body, and I just sat there looking like a human pincushion smoking a cigarette.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But my favorite was when I tried to quit by imaging every cigarette was a tiny man I was murdering. I killed so many tiny men, I had to see a therapist.

jokes.text: I watched you get hypnotized in Atlantic City. That guy did not hypnotize me, okay? You always pull your pants down and play 'Wipe Out' on your butt.
jokes.setup: Chandler insists hypnosis is 'beyond crap' and didn't work on him in Atlantic City
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals the specific humiliating detail — he played 'Wipe Out' on his own butt — which simultaneously confirms he was hypnotized AND that he has no memory of it
jokes.explanation: A very strong two-part joke. The specificity of 'Wipe Out' on the butt is inspired — it's both a visual gag and a character humiliation simultaneously. The structure is clean: denial → evidence that destroys the denial. The detail is weird enough to be original.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My father used to say the best way to quit smoking was to just stop buying cigarettes. Of course, he also used to say a lot of things while he was high. Like that time he told me he was a CIA agent who worked undercover as a street magician. Turns out he was just a guy who liked to juggle and disappear from his family for months at a time.

jokes.text: I was trying to distract attention from that poor, old woman who was trying to stuff her breasts into tube socks.
jokes.setup: Chandler is caught: Monica has proof he was hypnotized. He scrambles for an explanation.
jokes.punchline: He invents a bizarre, highly specific image — an old woman stuffing her breasts into tube socks — as a noble cover story
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler-specific escalation. Instead of accepting defeat, he doubles down with a more absurd lie. The image ('stuff her breasts into tube socks') is grotesque and specific in the best possible way. His framing of it as heroic — distraction for a poor woman's dignity — makes it funnier. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I couldn't call because my phone was broken. Then I had to walk to the store to get a new one, but I stepped in a puddle and my wallet fell out. By the time I fished it out, the store was closed. So I had to wait until morning, but then my alarm didn't go off because the power went out. When the power came back on, my clock was blinking 12:00, so I didn't know what time it was.

jokes.text: Forget hypnosis. The way to quit smoking is to dance naked in a field of heather and then bathe in the sweat of six healthy, young men.
jokes.setup: The group is debating how to help Chandler quit smoking
jokes.punchline: Phoebe offers her alternative remedy — naked field dancing followed by group sweat bathing — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe absurdist advice, delivered with total earnestness. The escalation from 'naked field dancing' to 'bathing in sweat of six healthy men' is well-constructed — each element more ridiculous. High character integration because only Phoebe says this as if it's reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: What happened to the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Frank Sr.
dialogue.line: It got wet.

jokes.text: Or what my father calls 'Thursday night.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes her naked-field-dancing smoking cure as if it's unusual
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals his father apparently does this every Thursday — making Phoebe's bizarre ritual suddenly mundane and making Chandler's upbringing seem spectacularly strange
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The economy is near-perfect: five words ('Or what my father calls') do an enormous amount of work. It simultaneously calls back to Phoebe's absurdist cure, adds dark dimension to Chandler's already-troubled backstory, and subverts the expectation that her ritual is exotic. The 'Thursday night' specificity is inspired — it implies regularity, routine, suggesting his father does this weekly. Strong candidate for standout moment. Justifies 8+ on every dimension.

jokes.text: I didn't want cinnamon on this. [Cut to Gunther apologizing to a customer]
jokes.setup: Scene opens in Central Perk; Gunther serves a customer
jokes.punchline: Gunther's only moment is a basic service failure — a comedic deflation that reestablishes his low-status role, played with his signature defeated energy
jokes.explanation: Weak scene-setting joke. Gunther screwing up a coffee order is extremely well-trodden for this show. No subversion, no escalation, just a mild character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Prostitution is illegal!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, that's what we've been saying.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no. It's illegal to pay for sex.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Right.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But it's legal to film it!

jokes.text: I would've called, but I lost your number. And then my mom locked me out of the house, so I couldn't find it. Then I tried to find a pay phone, and the receiver was cut off.
jokes.setup: Frank Jr. shows up unannounced; Rachel asks why he didn't call
jokes.punchline: Frank offers a cascading series of increasingly implausible excuses, each obstacle more absurd than the last, delivered with total obliviousness
jokes.explanation: A solid escalating-excuses joke that characterizes Frank Jr. immediately as a hapless disaster. The comedy is in his earnest delivery of a chain of failures. The 'Vandalism' callback is a nice structural touch.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.line: You're not what I pictured.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, most people aren't.

jokes.text: What happened? Vandalism. But also, what happened between you and your mom?
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks what happened to the pay phone receiver Frank tried to use
jokes.punchline: Frank matter-of-factly says 'Vandalism' — then Phoebe clarifies she was asking TWO questions, which Frank only answered one of
jokes.explanation: A tight two-beat joke. 'Vandalism' as a deadpan one-word answer works well, and Phoebe's gentle redirect ('But also...') is a clean structural move. Good economy.

dialogue.line: Sarcastic comment about the inappropriateness

jokes.text: I'd have bet good money that he'd be the first one of us to get married.
jokes.setup: Frank Jr. excitedly announces he's getting married
jokes.punchline: Ross says he'd have bet on Frank — a joke at Ross's own expense, given his own romantic failures, while simultaneously commenting on Frank's chaotic life
jokes.explanation: A mild self-aware joke about the group's romantic dysfunction, filtered through Ross's perspective. Functional but not especially clever.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I'm ready to have kids. I've thought about it a lot. I'm gonna break the cycle.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great, Frank. How exactly are you gonna break the cycle?

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: Well, I'm gonna be a great dad. I'm gonna give my kids everything I never had.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's wonderful.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: Yeah. Like, I'm gonna tell them that I love them every single day. And I'm gonna take them to the park, and I'm gonna teach them how to ride a bike. And I'm never, ever gonna hit them.

jokes.text: Well, he's 18. It'll be illegal for him to drink at his own bachelor party.
jokes.setup: Phoebe expresses concern that Frank is too young to get married
jokes.punchline: She quantifies it with a specific legal absurdity — he can't legally drink at his own bachelor party
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-constructed joke with a specific, original detail. The bachelor-party drinking angle is a fresh way to make the age point rather than saying it directly.

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.line: We realize there's an age difference between us.

jokes.text: Yeah, or to get a hooker. Always illegal, Joe.
jokes.setup: The group riffs on Frank being too young for bachelor party activities
jokes.punchline: Joey adds 'or to get a hooker' as an expected bachelor party activity; Chandler dryly corrects him that this is always illegal, not just at 18
jokes.explanation: A tight two-line joke with excellent character integration. Joey's obliviousness is completely on-brand, and Chandler's flat correction ('Always illegal, Joe') is one of his best deliveries in the episode. The joke is enhanced by the compressed structure — Chandler needs only three words to destroy Joey's logic.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You want to be set up? I can set you up!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, what about my friend, uh... oh wait, he's gay. What about... no, he's gay too. Oh! I got it! That guy... also gay.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, all your friends are gay!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I work in the fashion industry!

jokes.text: ...Mrs. Knight. [Frank introduces his fiancée, who is clearly much older than him]
jokes.setup: Frank announces 'this is my fiancée' with obvious excitement
jokes.punchline: The reveal is that his fiancée is a middle-aged woman — the name 'Mrs. Knight' itself signals her status as a former authority figure before we even see her
jokes.explanation: The reveal is the joke, and it's well-structured. The name 'Mrs. Knight' lands before any visual confirmation — the 'Mrs.' prefix alone tells you everything. In a multi-camera sitcom this would get a huge audience reaction. Solid structural comedy.

dialogue.line: Blunt assessment of shallow attraction reasons

jokes.text: You know, it's funny. Frank told me so much about you, but you're not how I pictured you at all.
jokes.setup: Alice meets Phoebe and tries to make pleasant small talk
jokes.punchline: She says Phoebe isn't 'how she pictured' — which is darkly ironic given that Phoebe is clearly the one doing the exact same shocked reassessment about Alice
jokes.explanation: A nice ironic reversal — the character who is clearly surprising everyone claims to be the one surprised. Works on two levels but isn't especially quotable.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm a big surprise.
jokes.setup: Alice hears that Phoebe didn't picture her as she appears
jokes.punchline: Alice drily acknowledges the obvious understatement of her being 'a big surprise' — self-aware humor that plays well given everyone's visible shock
jokes.explanation: Three words that do a lot of work. Alice's self-aware understatement signals she knows exactly what everyone is thinking. The brevity is its chief virtue.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, you dated Aunt Ruth?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, what's the big deal?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What's the big deal? She's our aunt!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She didn't tell me that at the time.

jokes.text: I was in her home-ec class. He was my best student. Yeah. She was my best teacher.
jokes.setup: The group asks how Frank and Alice met; they explain it was a teacher-student relationship
jokes.punchline: The mutual 'best student / best teacher' exchange is delivered with sweet, earnest pride — which makes it MORE disturbing, not less
jokes.explanation: Effective cringe comedy. The symmetric exchange ('best student / best teacher') is a well-structured cringe payoff — the more genuinely fond they are of each other, the more uncomfortable the audience feels.

jokes.text: If that doesn't keep kids in school, what will? [Reaction beat — Ross or another character stares after hearing the teacher-student romance]
jokes.setup: Frank and Alice describe their teacher-student romance with innocent pride
jokes.punchline: A deadpan observational comment notes the ironic 'incentive' — a teacher dating a student is not exactly a recommended school retention program
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-commentary joke. The irony is well-constructed: the very thing that should be a scandal is framed as an educational incentive. Clean, compact, dark-adjacent humor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm totally fine with the age difference. Age is just a number.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But when he told me he fought in Vietnam, I was like, okay, that's where I draw the line.

jokes.text: If that doesn't keep kids in school, what will?
jokes.setup: Frank has just revealed he fell in love with his home-ec teacher.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's mordant quip suggests the teacher-student romance is, ironically, a great incentive for school attendance — subverting the expected moral outrage with a dark observational twist.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The dark irony — treating the scandal as an education incentive — is sharp and unexpected. Perfect economy (one sentence), character-appropriate (Chandler's cynical wit), and it walks right up to an edgy line without crossing it. A standout line in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't believe you two are together! This is so wrong!

dialogue.speaker: Alice
dialogue.line: Phoebe, we're happy. Why can't you just be supportive?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because you're a paleontologist! You should know better than anyone that some things aren't meant to go together!

jokes.text: How hard can it be? You know, I mean, it's babies. Who doesn't want babies? Right?
jokes.setup: The group questions whether Frank is ready for children
jokes.punchline: Frank's breezy confidence — 'how hard can it be?' about raising children — reveals his total obliviousness in the most Frank-Jr.-possible way
jokes.explanation: Classic oblivious-character comedy. Frank's complete lack of self-awareness about parenthood is funny precisely because he's 18 and marrying his teacher. The rhetorical questions piling up add to his cluelessness.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, I haven't told him. Every time I try, I just end up saying something weird like 'Your hair smells like a thousand flowers' or 'I want to lick the inside of your ear.'

jokes.text: And besides, I never had a dad around. And now I always will, because it'll be me.
jokes.setup: Frank explains why he wants kids right away
jokes.punchline: His logic — 'I'll be my own kids' dad therefore I'll always have a dad' — is both genuinely sweet AND reveals a profound confusion about how fatherhood works relative to his own childhood longing
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly poignant joke that works on multiple levels. Frank's circular logic is both funny and sad — he's filling an emotional void with a misunderstanding of how parenthood works. The line earns its impact through character depth, not just setup-punchline mechanics.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: If I tell Frank, he'll feel terrible, and then he'll have to live with that for the rest of his life.

jokes.text: Good. Because you were acting like you didn't. [In response to Frank and Alice saying they're aware of the age difference]
jokes.setup: Frank and Alice note they are 'aware' of the age difference between them
jokes.punchline: Rachel drily fires back that their behavior suggested otherwise — a simple but effective straight-man reaction
jokes.explanation: A functional straight-man reaction. The economy is good (one line, clear payoff) but the joke itself is predictable — any audience member could write this response.

jokes.text: You are a strong, confident woman who does not need to smoke. A strong, confident woman.
jokes.setup: Chandler falls asleep listening to the hypnosis tape
jokes.punchline: The tape's affirmations are gendered — it keeps telling him he's a 'strong, confident WOMAN' — which we understand will have comic consequences later
jokes.explanation: This is the setup for the episode's main running gag. The joke of Chandler getting a women's empowerment tape is well-planted here. The audience immediately clocks the potential consequences. Scores higher in retrospect given payoff.

dialogue.line: Admission of pointless attachment to broken security

jokes.text: Not a problem. I work in fashion, and all I meet are eligible straight men.
jokes.setup: Monica asks Rachel to set her up with men since she's been out of the dating game
jokes.punchline: Rachel says she'll easily find eligible straight men in fashion — a notorious industry joke about the scarcity of straight men in fashion
jokes.explanation: A fairly dated stereotype joke about fashion and gay men. The irony is obvious and the joke leans on a cliché rather than earned subversion. Functional but below average craft.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's working! I feel like I can do anything!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey Monica, you look really... you have a great personality.

jokes.text: Cheesecake and a date, if you're giving them out.
jokes.setup: A waiter asks Pete if he wants anything else; he's clearly interested in Monica
jokes.punchline: Pete asks for 'cheesecake and a date' — pivoting from mundane diner order to bold flirtation in one beat
jokes.explanation: A charming and compact pickup-attempt joke. The double meaning of 'date' works well. Not groundbreaking but well-executed for a character introduction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So I left a tip at the restaurant...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I accidentally wrote in $500 instead of $5.

jokes.text: You wanna go out with me because of my wig, boobs, and because I serve you food. Well, if that were true, I'd be dating my Aunt Ruth.
jokes.setup: Monica lists the superficial reasons Pete would want to go out with her (wig, boobs, waitress)
jokes.punchline: Pete's response — 'I'd be dating my Aunt Ruth' — implies his aunt has all those same qualities, which is a brilliantly weird self-own
jokes.explanation: A clever and unexpected punchline. Pete's comeback works because it's so specific and self-deprecating in a sideways way — it doesn't refute Monica's list at all, it just reveals something strange about his aunt. Original and well-structured.

dialogue.line:
Looking at a photo
Revelation that the customer knows the President

jokes.text: That ain't a pretty picture in the morning. That wig all in disarray, and boobs flung over the nightstand.
jokes.setup: Joey imagines what it would look like if Ross pursued the waitress (Monica in disguise)
jokes.punchline: Joey paints a vivid, gleefully inappropriate morning-after visual — wig in disarray, prosthetic breasts thrown over furniture — with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A strong Joey joke. The image he conjures is both funny and strangely specific ('boobs flung over the nightstand'). His complete lack of filter is perfectly in character, and the physical comedy he's describing is vivid without being mean-spirited.

dialogue.line:
Discussing the age gap issue

Stark mathematical reality of the age difference

jokes.text: I don't wanna be judgmental, but it's sick. It's sick and wrong!
jokes.setup: Phoebe claims not to want to judge Frank's relationship with his older teacher-fiancée
jokes.punchline: She immediately judges it in the harshest possible terms — 'sick and wrong' — undercutting her 'non-judgmental' opener instantly
jokes.explanation: A classic sitcom irony structure (claim + immediate contradiction) executed with Phoebe's specific flavor of earnest outrage. The 'sick and wrong' repetition is energetic but the setup is predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: You know, Frank, you're a great guy. You just need to put yourself out there more.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: I mean, you're not conventionally attractive, but you have a great personality!

jokes.text: What, is it the age thing? I'm fine with the age thing... until it sticks its tongue down my little brother's throat.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Phoebe's objection is just about the age difference
jokes.punchline: Phoebe claims she's 'fine with the age thing' — then immediately specifies the precise moment she became not-fine, which is a viscerally specific image
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. The structure of 'I'm fine with X... until' is familiar but the specific payoff ('sticks its tongue down my little brother's throat') is viscerally funny. The grossness is earned because it's coming from a protective sibling's visceral horror.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: Is sex better with someone you care about?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wouldn't know.

jokes.text: You know what? It's not good home economics.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is ranting about how unfair Frank's situation is for him and the potential children
jokes.punchline: She concludes with a pun on 'home economics' — the subject Alice teaches — repurposing it as a general life-wisdom judgment
jokes.explanation: A clever wordplay callback. Phoebe recontextualizes Alice's actual subject as an ethical standard — 'not good home economics' as a life judgment. The pun is well-earned because the show has set up the home-ec connection. Above-average for a pun.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, he asked me to be best man, and I said yes because... we've been friends since high school. He's always been there for me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's beautiful, man.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it also doesn't hurt that his sister is incredibly hot.

jokes.text: Well, have you told him how you feel? Yes. Not out loud.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Phoebe if she's communicated her concerns to Frank
jokes.punchline: Phoebe says 'Yes' — then qualifies it with 'not out loud' — meaning she's only told him in her head
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. The structure is nearly perfect: 'Yes' gives a false sense of resolution; 'Not out loud' reframes everything in a single devastating qualifier. This is pure Phoebe — she literally considers thinking something the same as saying it. The economy is exceptional. Highly quotable, high character integration. Justifies an 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh no! This is a real mustard-tastrophe!

jokes.text: Pheebs, he's not a mind reader. We don't know that.
jokes.setup: Monica points out Frank can't know what Phoebe is thinking
jokes.punchline: Phoebe genuinely entertains the possibility that Frank might be a mind reader — delivered as a sincere possibility, not a joke
jokes.explanation: An excellent Phoebe joke. The callback to 'not out loud' is immediately paid off with her refusal to rule out mind-reading. 'We don't know that' is delivered with complete sincerity, which is the key. This is maximum character integration — only Phoebe would refuse to eliminate ESP as a communication pathway. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I didn't know how much to tip, so I just gave him what I thought was fair.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete, you tipped him $200 on a $15 sandwich! That's not fair, that's a down payment on a car!

jokes.text: Yeah, but if I do tell him, then he's gonna hate myself.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is worried about the consequences of telling Frank the truth
jokes.punchline: She mixes up her pronouns — 'he's gonna hate myself' instead of 'hate me' — a malapropism that reveals her emotional confusion while being accidentally funny
jokes.explanation: A soft malapropism joke that's more charming than hilarious. The pronoun error is very Phoebe but the comedy isn't particularly sharp — it reads more as a character texture beat than a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: You know, Monica and I have this thing where we fight about everything.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We do not fight about everything!

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: See? We're fighting right now.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not fighting, that's just us talking!

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Exactly. And that's how I know we're in love.

jokes.text: We're walking down the street, and I turn to you and say: 'Let's go hang out at Totally Nude Nudes.' Remember? And then you say, 'Let's just hang out at your place.'
jokes.setup: Joey is reminiscing about a time when Chandler chose staying home over going out
jokes.punchline: The bar Joey set was 'Totally Nude Nudes' — and Chandler STILL chose to go home, which implies Joey's 'nice move, dumb-ass' comment is fully warranted
jokes.explanation: A solid Joey-Chandler joke. 'Totally Nude Nudes' as an establishment name is funny by itself. Joey's genuine incredulity at Chandler's choice is good character comedy. The 'nice move, dumb-ass' button works well.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: That was the most romantic thing that's ever happened to me.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete, we were just fighting.

jokes.text: Well, that was a nice move, dumb-ass.
jokes.setup: Chandler turned down 'Totally Nude Nudes' to stay home
jokes.punchline: Joey's verdict — delivered as obvious fact — is both the punchline and a perfect encapsulation of Joey's worldview on male entertainment priorities
jokes.explanation: A good button with great economy. Joey's casual condemnation is funny but not particularly original. Works as a tag to joke 37.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Come on, just one meal. What do you say?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete, I can't.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I'll give you a hundred thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Two hundred thousand dollars!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Pete...

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Three hundred thousand dollars, and I'll throw in a lifetime supply of... what do you want?

jokes.text: Last Saturday night, what happened on Walker, Texas Ranger?
jokes.setup: Joey tries to convince Monica to go out with the guy rather than stay home
jokes.punchline: He asks what happened on Walker, Texas Ranger as evidence that she's wasting her Saturday nights — the show being so unhip it's a punchline in itself
jokes.explanation: A clean two-beat joke. 'Walker, Texas Ranger' as a symbol of staying home on Saturday night is well-chosen for the mid-90s context. The payoff — Monica answering in detail — confirms Joey's point instantly.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I was doing my laundry, and I realized that all my clothes were dark, so I figured I should just turn off all the lights in my apartment to match.

jokes.text: Well, Walker was looking for this big busload of kids.
jokes.setup: Joey has asked what Monica watched on Saturday night to prove she has no social life
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately and enthusiastically launches into a detailed Walker, Texas Ranger recap — proving Joey's point devastatingly well
jokes.explanation: The payoff to joke 39. Monica launching into the recap without hesitation is funnier than any denial could be. Her eagerness to share the plot is a great self-own that Joey's cutting gesture interrupts perfectly.

jokes.text: I forgot the combination to this about a year ago. I just carry it around.
jokes.setup: Gunther is shown carrying a combination lock
jokes.punchline: He casually admits he's been carrying a locked lock he can't open for an entire year — with no apparent plan to fix this
jokes.explanation: A strong Gunther joke. The specificity of 'about a year ago' plus 'I just carry it around' is perfectly absurd. It characterizes Gunther as someone who accepts inexplicable situations in his life — mirroring his acceptance of unrequited love for Rachel. Good character depth for a throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Maybe it's for the best.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: Yeah, the best. You know what 'best' means? It means I get to go back to living in a box under the bridge.

jokes.text: Good. I haven't smoked yet today. I feel great and confident. That is a stunning blouse.
jokes.setup: Monica asks how the hypnosis tape is working
jokes.punchline: Chandler says he feels 'great and confident' then immediately compliments Monica's blouse — the first sign the 'strong, confident woman' tape is feminizing him
jokes.explanation: The first payoff of the hypnosis running gag. The comedic machinery is smart: Chandler reports the tape is working perfectly, then immediately exhibits a side effect (complimenting the blouse like a woman would) without realizing the connection. The juxtaposition is clean and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: My wife thinks I'm lazy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: My kids don't respect me.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I can't hold down a job.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I'm going bald.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I think I have gout.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: There's a weird smell in my car.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: And I think my neighbor is stealing my newspapers.

jokes.text: As a joke, this customer who has a crush on me gave me a $20,000 tip.
jokes.setup: Monica describes Pete's tip as a 'joke'
jokes.punchline: The 'joke' is a $20,000 tip — establishing that Pete is so wealthy that sums this large are punchline-level frivolous for him
jokes.explanation: A functional comedy-of-wealth beat. The humor is in the disproportion — most people would call $20,000 anything but a joke. Sets up the Pete storyline effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: Your mom ever tie you to a radiator?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No!

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: Well, that's the difference.

jokes.text: Is this him? That's Bill Clinton. Who's he hugging? Oh, my God. That's Pete. Why is Bill hugging Pete?
jokes.setup: The group looks at a photo to identify Pete Becker
jokes.punchline: The photo has Bill Clinton in it, and Pete is the one hugging the President — establishing Pete's extraordinary wealth/connections through a single absurd image
jokes.explanation: A solid visual-gag joke. The reveal (Clinton in the photo) is unexpected, and the characters' collective bewilderment is funny. 'Why is Bill hugging Pete?' inverts the normal framing — it's Clinton doing the hugging, which implies Pete is the more important party.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I'm leaving! I'm done with you!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Frank, wait!

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: No! I can't... I can't actually leave. My car's in the shop and I don't have cab fare.

jokes.text: This guy invented Moss 865. Every office in the world uses that program. We use it! There you go! Monica's gonna go out with a millionaire.
jokes.setup: The friends research who Pete Becker is
jokes.punchline: Ross confirms Pete invented a major software program; Joey immediately reduces the news to 'Monica's going out with a millionaire' — a comically reductive but entirely Joey summary
jokes.explanation: A mild character beat. Joey's straight-to-the-money interpretation is funny and true to his character but not a particularly crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Pete! So... how much you make a year?

jokes.text: Or incredibly offensive. Yeah, sure. That too.
jokes.setup: Rachel is excited about the $20,000 check; Monica halfheartedly notes it's 'incredibly offensive'
jokes.punchline: Rachel dismisses the offense so quickly it's barely an afterthought — 'Yeah, sure. That too.' — revealing her priorities are entirely on the exciting side
jokes.explanation: A clean irony beat. The dismissal of the 'offensive' framing in two words is economical and true to Rachel's character at this stage.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: We flew to New York for pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You flew to New York for pizza?

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: It's really good pizza.

jokes.text: When you're 36, she's gonna be 88.
jokes.setup: The guys are trying to talk Frank out of marrying his 44-year-old teacher
jokes.punchline: Chandler does the specific math — when Frank is 36 (not even old), Alice will be 88 — a number so extreme it lands as dark comedy rather than logical argument
jokes.explanation: A well-structured joke that turns specific arithmetic into comedy. '88' at 36 is such a stark number that it's both accurate and darkly absurd. The economy is excellent — one sentence, no waste.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I have 10,000 rupees!

dialogue.speaker: Other character
dialogue.line: That's like $200.

jokes.text: What? You don't think I know that? All right, I'm gonna go play basketball. Or let the really good guys use my ball while I say, 'Can I play?'
jokes.setup: Frank gets emotional after the age-math argument and storms off
jokes.punchline: Instead of a dignified exit, Frank admits his 'storming off' will actually be a pathetic attempt to join a basketball game — immediately deflating any dramatic weight
jokes.explanation: A strong moment of character comedy. Frank's self-awareness about his own social standing (not good enough to join the basketball game) is unexpectedly touching and funny simultaneously. The specificity of 'letting the really good guys use my ball' is original and paints a vivid picture.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what, I'm gonna add my own suggestion to this thing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, here goes... 'You are a successful, talented, and incredibly attractive actor who gets every role he auditions for.'

jokes.text: The point is, there's a lot of women you haven't had sex with yet.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are trying to talk Frank out of marrying young
jokes.punchline: Chandler cuts through all the philosophical discussion to reduce the argument to the most basic possible terms — unslept-with women — as if this is the essential wisdom Frank needs
jokes.explanation: A functional joke that fits Chandler's brand of accidental crudeness. Not especially original but lands well in context as a comic deflation of more earnest arguments.

jokes.text: Isn't sex better when it's with one person that you really care about? Yeah, in a poem, maybe.
jokes.setup: Frank Jr. makes a romantic argument for committed love over promiscuity
jokes.punchline: Joey dismisses Frank's sentiment with brutal pragmatism — 'Yeah, in a poem, maybe' — suggesting the idea is fictional romanticism
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Yeah, in a poem, maybe' is a near-perfect line: economical, character-specific, and surprisingly sharp. Only Joey — who genuinely believes meaningless sex is superior — could deliver this with such confident authority. The 'maybe' qualifier is perfect, leaving just a crack of doubt. Very quotable, high craft, justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: No, the man's right. That's what I had with Rachel. You don't have it anymore? No. I slept with someone else.
jokes.setup: Ross endorses Frank's romantic view of sex, citing his relationship with Rachel as an example
jokes.punchline: Frank innocently asks if Ross still has that, and Ross's answer — 'No. I slept with someone else' — is both a devastating reveal and a great comic compression of his infidelity
jokes.explanation: Sharp writing. Ross builds himself up romantically only to deflate himself in one sentence. 'No. I slept with someone else.' is a beautifully blunt confession compressed into five words, delivered in front of someone he barely knows. The dark humor comes from the disproportionate context.

jokes.text: All right! Congratulations, you lucky bastard! You're Frank's best man?
jokes.setup: Frank's emotional speech about his love for Alice wins over Joey
jokes.punchline: Joey is so moved by Frank's love speech that he becomes Frank's best man — despite having come to talk him OUT of the wedding
jokes.explanation: A good ironic reversal. Joey is sent to talk Frank out of the wedding and ends up as best man. 'I couldn't help it. Their love is so pure' is a characteristically Joey explanation. Chandler's follow-up 'You're Frank's best man?' is the necessary straight-man confirmation.

jokes.text: I couldn't help it. Their love is so pure.
jokes.setup: Chandler reacts in disbelief that Joey is now Frank's best man
jokes.punchline: Joey defends himself with 'Their love is so pure' — a phrase that sounds absurd defending a relationship between an 18-year-old and his 44-year-old teacher
jokes.explanation: A strong Joey line. The unintentional irony of 'their love is so pure' describing a teacher-student romance that everyone else finds disturbing is the core of the joke. Joey's complete sincerity is the delivery mechanism.

jokes.text: What about you, huh? I'm the ring bearer.
jokes.setup: After revealing Joey is best man, Chandler is asked what role he's taking at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Chandler is the ring bearer — a position normally held by a young child — which he accepts without shame
jokes.explanation: A clean, compact joke. The ring bearer revelation is perfectly timed and the economy is excellent — four words. The joke is that BOTH guys failed their anti-wedding mission and ended up with wedding roles, but Chandler's role is more demeaning (child's role). The delivery implies he can't even explain how it happened.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Who died on this? Yeah, I know. It's a real 'mustard-tastrophe.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe pretends to need home-ec help to get Alice alone; Alice sees a badly stained garment
jokes.punchline: Alice describes the stain as a 'mustard-tastrophe' — a portmanteau that is simultaneously groan-worthy and reveals Alice's earnest home-ec teacher persona
jokes.explanation: A fun wordplay joke. 'Mustard-tastrophe' is a decent pun that works because it's so earnestly Alice — a home-ec teacher would coin a word like this and mean it. The setup ('who died on this?') is also a nice bit from Phoebe.

jokes.text: Never say that. If you can't get it out, cut around the stain, add a little lace, you make a stylish throw.
jokes.setup: Alice gives sincere, detailed home-ec stain advice
jokes.punchline: Her solution escalates from practical (club soda and salt) to absurd (cut around the stain, add lace, make a throw) — all delivered with genuine home-ec authority
jokes.explanation: A good character joke for Alice. Her earnest commitment to home-ec problem-solving, including impractical solutions delivered with total confidence, characterizes her well.

jokes.text: Or instead, maybe you could just not marry my brother Frank?
jokes.setup: Alice has just given detailed, earnest stain advice; Phoebe has been building to her real agenda
jokes.punchline: Phoebe pivots from stain removal to 'don't marry my brother' in a single breezy sentence, as if it's the same category of domestic suggestion
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured scene pivot. The joke works because of the jarring tonal contrast: practical domestic advice immediately followed by 'or just don't marry my brother.' The breezy casualness of 'Or instead, maybe you could just' is what makes it land — Phoebe treats them as equivalent suggestions. High structure score, good character integration.

jokes.text: Can we make it smaller? Make it fit on the head of a pin? I love when we make things fit on the head of a pin.
jokes.setup: Pete is shown in a tech context, apparently working on something with an engineer
jokes.punchline: He casually asks to miniaturize something to fit on a pin head — technobabble delivered with Silicon Valley billionaire nonchalance — plus 'I love when we do that' makes it a recurring quirk
jokes.explanation: A mild but charming joke establishing Pete as a quirky tech billionaire who delights in impossible engineering challenges. 'I love when we make things fit on the head of a pin' is an amusingly specific joy.

jokes.text: You double the tax. Not double the tax of Romania.
jokes.setup: Monica confronts Pete about the obscene $20,000 tip
jokes.punchline: She explains the standard tipping convention (double the tax), then specifies Pete's mistake as having doubled a hypothetical Romanian tax rate — implying the math is laughably wrong
jokes.explanation: A sharp, original joke. The Romania comparison is an unexpected and specific way to convey the absurdity of the tip amount. 'Not double the tax of Romania' is quotable and the kind of line that sticks. Monica's delivery as a professional who knows exactly how tipping works makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I'm still here. [Pete's employee who has been sitting in on the meeting remains present while Monica confronts Pete]
jokes.setup: Monica bursts in to confront Pete about the tip; his employee is still in the room
jokes.punchline: The employee awkwardly notes he's still there — acknowledging the suddenly personal conversation he's now trapped in
jokes.explanation: A functional awkward-presence joke. Three words, good timing. A bit thin on its own but it works as situational comedy.

jokes.text: You're taking this wrong. If I didn't leave you that tip, you wouldn't have come, we wouldn't have this argument, and there wouldn't be this heat between us. You gotta admit that our relationship is hitting a new level now.
jokes.setup: Monica confronts Pete for the offensive tip
jokes.punchline: Pete reframes her angry confrontation as evidence of romantic chemistry — calling her fury 'heat between us' and their fight a relationship 'hitting a new level'
jokes.explanation: Pete's delusional optimism is funny and slightly endearing. The reframing of a confrontation as intimacy is a classic romantic-comedy beat but executed with a specific and charming Pete quality.

jokes.text: You were the chef and I was the customer. But now we're, like, this couple that fights.
jokes.setup: Pete continues reframing his relationship with Monica
jokes.punchline: He describes 'a couple that fights' as an achieved relationship milestone — as if going from strangers to an arguing couple is romantic progress
jokes.explanation: A mild absurdist joke about Pete's warped romantic logic. 'We're like this couple that fights' as a POSITIVE development is funny in its audacity. Pete's obliviousness is charming.

jokes.text: You're a loon.
jokes.setup: Pete has just told Monica that their angry confrontation is them 'hitting a new level' as a couple
jokes.punchline: Monica's verdict — 'You're a loon' — is a perfectly compressed reaction, delivered flat
jokes.explanation: Three words. Perfect economy. 'Loon' is a slightly old-fashioned word choice that feels very Monica — precise and slightly exasperated. Works as a great button on Pete's romantic delusion.

jokes.text: We go out, we eat. If you don't have a good time, I'll give you 10 grand, we're even.
jokes.setup: Pete is trying to convince Monica to go out with him after the tip drama
jokes.punchline: He offers to pay her $10,000 if she doesn't have a good time — as if money solves all disputes, and as if $10K is a reasonable dinner wager
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the money-as-solution motif. Pete's instinct to compensate with cash for any friction is an established character quirk by this point, and $10,000 as a 'we're even' amount is absurdly reasonable-seeming from his perspective.

jokes.text: Well, your laundry smelled so good that I thought I'd curl up in it.
jokes.setup: Rachel finds Chandler in her apartment, hiding in her laundry in the dark
jokes.punchline: Chandler explains he was sitting in her laundry because it smelled good — a bizarre, slightly infantile behavior he offers as a perfectly reasonable explanation
jokes.explanation: The hypnosis tape's side effects are now producing stranger behavior — Chandler curling up in Rachel's laundry. The joke is enhanced by knowing the tape is making him behave in stereotypically 'womanly' comfort-seeking ways. Works well in context of the running gag.

jokes.text: Yeah, yeah. No. I don't know. But you know what? Maybe it's just all for the best. Well, yeah, if the best is, like, unbelievable pain.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to offer hollow comfort that Alice breaking up with Frank is 'for the best'
jokes.punchline: Frank cuts through the platitude: 'Well yeah, if the best is, like, unbelievable pain' — a darkly funny riposte to empty comfort
jokes.explanation: A nice dark joke that reveals Frank's emotional depth. His reframing of 'for the best' as equivalent to 'unbelievable pain' is both sad and funny — a teenage boy's very real heartbreak delivered with accidentally sharp comedic timing.

jokes.text: ...and then getting arrested for stealing those birds, and then the whole punctured-lung thing.
jokes.setup: Frank is explaining his difficult life before Alice
jokes.punchline: His backstory escalates from absent dad to arrested-for-stealing-birds to punctured lung — each revelation more absurd and specific than the last, delivered as a matter-of-fact biography
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. 'Getting arrested for stealing birds' is a beautifully specific absurd detail that perfectly characterizes Frank Jr.'s chaotic life. The escalation to 'punctured lung thing' delivered as an afterthought is equally good. The writing makes Frank both funny and sympathetic simultaneously — a difficult balance.

jokes.text: It's still really hard to take deep breaths in cold weather.
jokes.setup: Frank mentions the punctured lung as one of his life hardships
jokes.punchline: He adds the specific physical consequence — trouble breathing deeply in cold weather — with casual matter-of-factness, as if this is just a minor inconvenience in his litany of disasters
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the punctured lung revelation. The specificity ('cold weather') and deadpan delivery make a medical aftermath funny. Only Frank Jr. would mention a still-impaired lung this casually as a footnote to a breakup conversation.

jokes.text: My mother didn't want us to be together, but the worst thing she ever did was tie me to the porch.
jokes.setup: Frank has just learned Phoebe broke up his engagement; he's processing his anger
jokes.punchline: He compares Phoebe's interference to his mother's 'worst' opposition — which was tying him to the porch — revealing an extraordinarily dysfunctional family while also suggesting Phoebe's betrayal is worse
jokes.explanation: An excellent dark joke. 'The worst thing she ever did was tie me to the porch' is a perfectly calibrated Frank Jr. line — it reveals his upbringing as casually abusive while his delivery treats it as a minor comparison point. The dark humor is fully earned by the character, not cheaply inserted. The implicit message that Phoebe has done WORSE than being tied to a porch is an effective comedic escalation. Justifies 8+ on character integration and originality.

jokes.text: You know, I would storm out of here if I had some money or a place to go.
jokes.setup: Frank is furious at Phoebe and clearly wants to make a dramatic exit
jokes.punchline: He can't storm out because he has no money and no place to go — his angry declaration is immediately deflated by his own helplessness
jokes.explanation: A standout joke. The structure is superb: the setup is a classic TV dramatic moment (character about to storm out in anger), and the punchline completely collapses it by acknowledging Frank's absolute powerlessness. 'Some money or a place to go' covers all his deficiencies in six words. High character integration — this is entirely Frank Jr. Dark, sweet, and funny simultaneously. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: Ross, if you had a million dollars, what's the first thing you'd buy? I'd get some municipal bonds, put the rest in the bank, and live off the interest.
jokes.setup: Joey asks Ross a classic fantasy question to assess his fun level
jokes.punchline: Ross's answer — municipal bonds and bank interest — is the least imaginative, most financially responsible, and therefore funniest possible response to 'what would you do with a million dollars'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed character joke. The comedy is in the total mismatch between the spirit of the question and Ross's hyper-responsible answer. 'Municipal bonds' is a perfectly chosen specific — it's boring but correct, which is quintessential Ross. High character integration.

jokes.text: Well, we've heard from Dr. Fun.
jokes.setup: Ross has given the most boring possible answer to the fun hypothetical
jokes.punchline: Joey's sarcastic nickname 'Dr. Fun' for Ross is a perfect encapsulation of Ross's joyless practicality
jokes.explanation: Excellent button. 'Dr. Fun' is a brilliantly economical sarcastic label that perfectly captures Ross's personality. The 'Well, we've heard from' framing — as if Ross is a panelist who has delivered his expert testimony — adds an extra layer of irony. High quotability and economy. Joey delivers this kind of zinger better than any other character.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! The millionaire's here! / Oh, my God!
jokes.setup: Pete arrives at the apartment while they're mid-conversation about him.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe and Rachel's joint excited freakout — 'The millionaire's here!' — is funny in Phoebe's choice of title ('the millionaire,' as if it's his formal designation) and the shared hysteria.
jokes.explanation: Mild but charming. 'The millionaire' as Pete's title is the joke — treating his wealth as an identity. Functional crowd-pleaser.

jokes.text: Okay, just because he buys you dinner does not mean you owe him anything. I know. Okay, then get the lobster.
jokes.setup: Rachel gives Monica a feminist pep talk before her date with the millionaire
jokes.punchline: She immediately undermines her own 'you don't owe him anything' speech by adding 'get the lobster' — the most expensive item, betraying her real motivation
jokes.explanation: A sharp two-beat joke with a clean ironic reversal. Rachel's self-contradiction is rapid and well-timed — she doesn't even pause between 'you don't owe him anything' and 'get the lobster.' The joke works on character too: Rachel's materialistic side is an established trait. Good economy.

jokes.text: How much cash you got in your pocket now?
jokes.setup: Pete arrives to pick up Monica for their date; Joey and Chandler are there
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately asks Pete how much cash he has — the most direct possible way to determine someone's wealth — with zero social filter
jokes.explanation: A concise character beat. Joey's complete lack of social awareness about money is perfectly rendered. The joke is in the directness — no preamble, no social lubricant.

jokes.text: And that's why I'm not inviting you in for a drink. Bye.
jokes.setup: Joey has just asked Pete how much cash he's carrying the moment they meet
jokes.punchline: Pete immediately connects Joey's rude question to his decision not to invite them in — a perfectly rational response that he delivers without breaking stride
jokes.explanation: A clean button. Pete's dry causality ('that's why') is funny because he's completely right and he knows it. Good economy.

jokes.text: You're not paying for the pizza. Come on, it's only fair. You paid for the flight.
jokes.setup: Monica insists on paying for pizza on their date to establish equality
jokes.punchline: Pete says it's only fair she let him pay since he paid for 'the flight' — implying he flew her somewhere for a first date pizza, a completely disproportionate expenditure she apparently didn't flag
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed joke that uses the reveal structure effectively. The casual mention of 'the flight' as if it's normal is a great Pete moment — he took her on a plane for pizza and considers this an unremarkable dating expense.

jokes.text: Is that enough lira? I'd throw another 1000 on that. How much is that? That's about 60 cents.
jokes.setup: Monica and Pete are splitting a pizza tab in what appears to be Italy
jokes.punchline: Pete's generous 'throw another 1000 on that' sounds lavish until Monica (or Pete) clarifies it's about 60 cents — deflating the gesture completely through currency exchange
jokes.explanation: A solid setup-punchline joke. The deflation of '1000 lira' to '60 cents' is a clean reveal. The joke works well because Pete has been positioned as absurdly wealthy, making the accidental cheapness of lira funny.

jokes.text: Every night! [Chandler watching TV with apparent enthusiasm]
jokes.setup: Chandler is seen alone at night, watching TV
jokes.punchline: His enthusiastic 'Every night!' suggests he's celebrating something on TV — likely a woman-oriented show or product, continuing the hypnosis tape's effect of making him behave in stereotypically feminine ways
jokes.explanation: A visual running-gag beat. Without full context, the joke relies on what the audience sees (likely a shopping channel or similar female-targeted content). Works as part of the hypnosis tape arc.

jokes.text: So can I. (Chandler responding to the tape's 'strong, confident woman' — implying he too can go without smoking, in a female voice/manner)
jokes.setup: The hypnosis tape continues: 'You are a strong, confident woman who does not need to smoke.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's half-asleep agreement 'So can I' suggests he has fully absorbed the female identity from the tape and is identifying with the 'strong, confident woman' while also showing the tape is working.
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff for the running gag. 'So can I' is maximally economical — two words that confirm he has merged with the 'strong, confident woman' persona. The ambiguity (is he saying he can quit smoking? Is he saying he IS a strong confident woman?) is the joke's richness.

jokes.text: Hi, Frank. Hi, Mrs. Knight.
jokes.setup: Frank answers the door expecting Phoebe; instead Alice is there, presumably to reconcile
jokes.punchline: Frank instinctively reverts to 'Mrs. Knight' — his teacher — the moment he's emotionally caught off guard, revealing the habit is still deeply ingrained even in their romantic relationship
jokes.explanation: A strong callback to the teacher-student dynamic. Frank's involuntary 'Mrs. Knight' in a highly emotional moment is both funny and characterful — it shows the relationship's dynamic hasn't fully escaped the teacher-student framing even for Frank.

jokes.text: All right, that's a goodbye kiss. That's good. Bye-bye. But no, the important thing is, is that you see what I'm saying.
jokes.setup: Frank and Alice share what is supposed to be a final goodbye kiss; Phoebe is watching
jokes.punchline: Phoebe nervously narrates and moderates the goodbye kiss — calling it 'that's good' as if coaching them — then tries to redirect to her moral point, completely ignoring the emotional moment
jokes.explanation: A cringe-comedy beat where Phoebe's discomfort at the intimacy she's witnessing leads her to narrate and coach it. 'Bye-bye' as a parting instruction is a funny deflation of the dramatic moment.

jokes.text: This is clearly wrong. I've decided I'm gonna let this happen.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just orchestrated the breakup and is watching the goodbye — but then Frank and Alice start kissing again
jokes.punchline: Phoebe instantly abandons her entire moral stance ('This is clearly wrong') and reverses to 'I'm gonna let this happen' — indicating she's moved by what she sees even though she disagrees with it
jokes.explanation: A strong character reversal. Phoebe's immediate about-face from 'wrong' to 'let this happen' is funny because of the gap between her principles and her emotional response. It's also very Phoebe — her heart always overrides her logic.

jokes.text: Joey's your best friend. You wanna make him a cheese sandwich every day. You wanna buy him hundreds of dollars' worth of pants.
jokes.setup: The hypnosis tape's suggestions are now leaking into Chandler's behavior even when awake
jokes.punchline: The tape has replaced 'be a strong confident woman who doesn't smoke' with suggestions about Joey — Chandler now wants to make Joey sandwiches and buy him pants, suggesting the tape has been tampered with or looped strangely
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and the best payoff of the hypnosis running gag. The specificity of 'cheese sandwich every day' and 'hundreds of dollars' worth of pants' is inspired — these are perfectly Joey-specific gifts that only make sense if Joey has been secretly influencing the tape. The joke caps the whole arc with a completely original, highly quotable ending. The structure is near-perfect: the tape arc has been building all episode, and this final revelation recontextualizes everything while adding new comedy. Strong candidate for the episode's best joke. Justifies 8+ on all dimensions.

tmdb_overview: Monica receives a tip from an admirer worth a small fortune then goes out with the guy. A hypnosis tape intended to assist Chandler to stop smoking has a rather strange side effect. Phoebe is upset when her 18-year-old half-brother, Frank Jr., makes a surprise announcement that he is getting married - to a woman more than twice his age.
insight: Hypnosis tape premise stretches thin across 49 jokes at middling 2.5-per-minute pace.
